chapters.title: Complexity science
chapters.tagline: The numpy toolkit, and your first emergent model: Schelling's city in one line of houses
goals: Build and slice numpy arrays, and use boolean masks to count things
Look at a cell's neighbours with np.roll instead of fiddly index loops
Write a complete agent model (a 1-D Schelling city) from rules to plot
Name the shifts that separate complexity science from classical science

blocks.html:
In the 3D lab you moved unhappy households by hand and watched a city split into red and blue clusters. In this track you write the code that does it.

Every chapter climbs the same ladder: run the book's code, predict what a program prints, reorder scrambled lines, fill blanks, hunt a bug, write a function against checks, then rebuild the chapter's core idea from memory and explain it in words. It feels slower than reading. It's the part that makes it stick.
From the 3D world: Chapter 1's city is the same model you'll build here, flattened to a single street so every line of code is easy to see. Open the City world
Tip: every grey code box is editable. Press Ctrl + Enter (or ⌘ + Enter) to run it. Break things on purpose; Reset puts the original back.

sections.title: Arrays: the bricks of every model

blocks.html: Almost every model in Think Complexity is a numpy array that changes over time: a row of cells, a grid of sand, a city of households. Three moves cover most of what you need: make an array, look at part of it, and ask a yes/no question of every element at once.

blocks.code:
city = np.array([1, 2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 2])   # 0 empty, 1 red, 2 blue
print(city[2:5])          # a slice: elements 2, 3, 4
print(city == 1)          # a boolean mask: one True/False per house
print(np.sum(city == 1))  # True counts as 1, so this counts red houses
print(city[city != 0])    # use a mask to keep only occupied houses
blocks.title: Make, slice, ask

opts.t: 1, because the first house is red
0.5, the fraction of houses that are red
An error: you can't average booleans

blocks.why: city == 1 is [True, False, False, True]. numpy treats True as 1 and False as 0, so the mean is 2/4 = 0.5. "Mean of a mask" = "fraction that satisfy the condition", a pattern you'll use in every chapter.

blocks.title: Occupancy report
blocks.prompt: Fill the blanks so report(city) returns the number of empty houses and the fraction of occupied houses that are red.
blocks.tests:
empty, frac = report(np.array([1, 2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 2]))
assert empty == 2, f"Expected 2 empty houses, got {empty}"
assert abs(frac - 0.5) < 1e-9, f"3 of the 6 occupied houses are red, so expect 0.5, got {frac}"
assert report(np.array([1, 0, 0]))[1] == 1.0, "Empty houses must not count toward the red fraction"
hints: The first blank is a condition that is True for empty houses.
The second blank is a mask that keeps only houses that are not empty: city != 0.
blocks.starter:
def report(city):
    empty = np.sum(____)
    occupied = city[____]
    frac_red = np.mean(occupied == 1)
    return empty, frac_red
blocks.solution:
def report(city):
    empty = np.sum(city == 0)
    occupied = city[city != 0]
    frac_red = np.mean(occupied == 1)
    return empty, frac_red

blocks.html: A Schelling household looks at the houses around it. With a loop you'd write city[i-1], city[i+1] and then worry about the ends of the street. np.roll shifts the whole array at once and wraps around, so the street becomes a ring with no ends to special-case.

blocks.code:
city = np.array([1, 2, 0, 1, 1])
print("city      ", city)
print("roll(+1)  ", np.roll(city, 1))    # each position now holds its LEFT neighbour
print("roll(-1)  ", np.roll(city, -1))   # ... its RIGHT neighbour
same_left = (np.roll(city, 1) == city) & (city != 0)
print("same as left?", same_left)
blocks.title: Rolling the street
Count same-colour neighbours
blocks.prompt:
Write same_neighbors(city, r=1). For every house, count how many of the houses within distance r on each side (so 2*r houses) have the same colour. The street is a ring. Empty houses should get 0, and empty neighbours never count.

Use np.roll inside a loop over the offsets -r … r (skip 0).
blocks.tests:
c = np.array([1, 1, 2, 0, 2, 2])
got = same_neighbors(c, 1)
assert got.tolist() == [1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1], f"r=1: expected [1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1], got {got.tolist()}"
got2 = same_neighbors(c, 2)
assert got2.tolist() == [1, 1, 1, 0, 2, 1], f"r=2: expected [1, 1, 1, 0, 2, 1], got {got2.tolist()}"
assert same_neighbors(np.array([0, 0, 0]), 1).tolist() == [0, 0, 0], "Empty houses have no neighbours of their own colour"
hints: For each offset d, np.roll(city, d) lines every house up with one neighbour. Compare it with city.
Mask out empty houses with & (city != 0): otherwise two empty houses next to each other would count as "same".
blocks.starter:
def same_neighbors(city, r=1):

blocks.html:
Here are the rules, exactly as in the 3D city but on one street:

  1. Each house is empty (0), red (1) or blue (2). The street wraps around.
  2. A household looks at the 2r houses around it. It is happy if at least a fraction p of its occupied neighbours share its colour (or if it has no neighbours at all).
  3. Each step, every unhappy household moves to a random empty house.

blocks.title: Who is unhappy?
blocks.prompt: same_neighbors from above is already defined for you. Fill in the blanks of unhappy, which returns a boolean mask that is True for unhappy households.
blocks.tests:
c = np.array([1, 2, 1, 0, 2, 2])
u = unhappy(c, 0.5, 1)
assert u.dtype == bool, "Return a boolean mask"
assert u.tolist() == [True, True, True, False, False, False], f"Expected [True, True, True, False, False, False], got {u.tolist()}"
assert not unhappy(np.array([0, 1, 0, 0]), 0.5, 1).any(), "A household with no neighbours is happy"
assert unhappy(np.array([1, 1, 2, 2]), 0.6, 1).tolist() == [True, True, True, True], "With p=0.6 a 1-of-2 match is not enough"
hints: Two conditions: the house is occupied, and its fraction of same-colour neighbours is below p.

blocks.html: Now the step function. Before you write it, rebuild it from scrambled lines. Watch for the decoy.
The full model, with a plot. Run it, then change p to 0.3 and to 0.7.

blocks.title: Watch the street sort itself
Rebuild the segregation measure
blocks.prompt: From memory: write segregation(city, r), the average fraction of same-colour neighbours over every occupied house that has at least one occupied neighbour. same_neighbors and occupied_neighbors are available.
blocks.tests:
assert segregation(np.array([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2]), 1) is not None, "Return a number"
assert abs(segregation(np.array([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2]), 1) - 2/3) < 1e-9, "Two clean blocks of three: every house has 1 of 2 or 2 of 2 alike, average 2/3"
assert abs(segregation(np.array([1, 2, 1, 2]), 1) - 0.0) < 1e-9, "Perfectly alternating: no neighbour is alike"
assert abs(segregation(np.array([1, 1, 0, 2]), 1) - 0.5) < 1e-9, "Divide by occupied neighbours only (here the scores are 1/2, 1/1 and 0/1, so the average is 0.5)"
hints: Build a mask of houses that are occupied and have occupied_neighbors > 0, then average same / occupied over just those houses.

blocks.title: The happy-everyone bug
blocks.prompt: This version of unhappy returns a mask, runs without errors, and is wrong: in a mixed street almost nobody is ever unhappy. Find the bug and fix it.
blocks.tests:
c = np.array([1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2])
assert unhappy(c, 0.5, 1).all(), "In a perfectly alternating street every household has 0 alike neighbours, so all are unhappy"
assert not unhappy(np.array([1, 1, 1, 1]), 0.5, 1).any(), "All-red street: nobody is unhappy"
assert unhappy(np.array([1, 0, 2, 2]), 0.5, 1).tolist() == [True, False, False, False], "Divide by occupied neighbours, not by 2r: house 2 has one occupied neighbour and it matches"
hints: There are two bugs hiding in two lines. Look at the comparison operator first: unhappy means below the threshold.
The second bug: dividing by 2 * r counts empty houses as "not alike". Schelling's rule uses the fraction of occupied neighbours.

blocks.html: The book's first chapter describes a set of shifts away from classical, equation-based science. Your street model shows several of them at once: it's discrete (houses, not a smooth density), stochastic (random moves), made of many interacting agents, and studied by computation (you ran it) rather than by analysis (solving for an answer on paper).

blocks.q: Which pair best describes the move from classical models to the Schelling model?

opts.t: From one or two bodies described by equations, to many simple agents studied by simulation

blocks.why: Classical physics models a few bodies with equations you can solve. Schelling's model has hundreds of agents with a simple rule, and the interesting result, strong clustering from mild preferences, appears only when you run it. That is the core shift the book describes.

blocks.q: Nobody in the model wants a segregated street (at p = 0.5 everyone is fine with half their neighbours being different). Yet the street segregates. What is the name for a pattern at the level of the whole system that no individual rule mentions?
blocks.why: Emergence: the system-level property (large single-colour blocks) is not written into any agent's rule. You saw it appear in the plot.

blocks.q: In your own words: why does a city segregate strongly even when each household is happy with half its neighbours being different?
blocks.a:
• A household that moves leaves a gap and lands somewhere new, which changes the neighbourhood of several other households.
  • Moves are local and keep cascading: each move can make a neighbour unhappy, who then moves too.
  • The system only stops when (almost) nobody is unhappy, and the configurations where nobody is unhappy are mostly clustered ones. Mild individual preferences + feedback = strong collective pattern.

blocks.q: Why use np.roll instead of a loop with city[i-1] and city[i+1]?
blocks.a:
• It handles the whole array at once (fast, short code).
  • It wraps around, so the ends of the street need no special case: the street is a ring.
  • np.roll(city, d) lines every house up with its neighbour at offset d, so one comparison checks every house.

chapters.title: Graphs
chapters.tagline: Build graphs with NetworkX, search them, and find the tipping point of random graphs
goals: Make graphs with NetworkX and walk their neighbours
Write generator functions like the book's all_pairs and random_pairs
Implement reachable_nodes (graph search with a stack) and is_connected
Generate Erdős–Rényi graphs and measure the jump in connectivity near p* = ln(n)/n
chapters.prelude:
import numpy as np
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

blocks.html: A graph is a set of nodes and the edges between them. NetworkX gives you a Graph object; you add nodes and edges, then ask questions.
From the 3D world: the Party is a graph. Guests are nodes, a conversation is an edge, and you found the moment when "lots of little chats" turns into "everyone is connected". Open the Party

blocks.code:
G = nx.Graph()
G.add_nodes_from(["Alice", "Bob", "Chuck", "Dana"])
G.add_edge("Alice", "Bob")
G.add_edge("Alice", "Chuck")
G.add_edge("Bob", "Chuck")
print("nodes:", list(G.nodes))
print("edges:", list(G.edges))
print("Alice knows:", list(G.neighbors("Alice")))
print("Dana knows:", list(G.neighbors("Dana")))
nx.draw_circular(G, with_labels=True, node_color="#c9d3f5", node_size=1400)
blocks.title: A tiny social graph

blocks.q: In an undirected graph with n nodes, how many edges does the complete graph (every node linked to every other) have?
blocks.why: Each of the n nodes links to n-1 others, giving n(n-1) ends of edges, and every edge has two ends, so n(n-1)/2 edges. With 10 guests that's 45 conversations.

blocks.html: The book builds graphs from generator functions: functions that yield values one at a time instead of building a whole list.

blocks.title: The book's all_pairs
The double-counting bug
blocks.prompt: This all_pairs runs fine and a complete graph built from it even looks right. But it yields every pair twice (once as (u, v), once as (v, u)) and one pair that isn't a pair at all. Later, when we flip a coin for each pair, that silently changes the probability of an edge. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
pairs = list(all_pairs(range(5)))
assert all(u != v for u, v in pairs), "A node paired with itself would be a self-loop"
assert len(pairs) == 10, f"5 nodes have 5*4/2 = 10 pairs; you yielded {len(pairs)}"
assert len(set(frozenset(p) for p in pairs)) == 10, "Each pair should appear once"
hints: Compare the indexes i and j, not the values. Which condition keeps exactly one of (i, j) and (j, i), and drops i == j?

blocks.title: make_complete_graph
blocks.prompt: Fill in the blanks to build a complete graph with nodes 0 … n-1. all_pairs is defined for you.
blocks.tests:
G = make_complete_graph(10)
assert G.number_of_nodes() == 10, "Expected 10 nodes"
assert G.number_of_edges() == 45, f"A complete graph on 10 nodes has 45 edges, got {G.number_of_edges()}"
assert make_complete_graph(1).number_of_nodes() == 1, "A single node with no edges is still a graph with one node"
blocks.starter:
def make_complete_graph(n):
    G = nx.Graph()
    nodes = range(n)
    G.add_nodes_from(____)
    G.add_edges_from(____)
    return G
blocks.solution:
def make_complete_graph(n):
    G = nx.Graph()
    nodes = range(n)
    G.add_nodes_from(nodes)
    G.add_edges_from(all_pairs(nodes))
    return G

blocks.html: A graph is connected if you can get from any node to any other by following edges. The book's algorithm: start somewhere, mark it seen, then keep visiting neighbours of things you've seen until there's nothing new.

blocks.title: reachable_nodes, the book's version
blocks.prompt: Rebuild the search. A stack holds nodes we have found but not processed; seen holds nodes we've processed.

blocks.code:
def reachable_nodes(G, start):
    seen = set()
    stack = [start]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        if node not in seen:
            seen.add(node)
            stack.extend(G.neighbors(node))
    return seen

G = nx.Graph([(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 5)])
print(sorted(reachable_nodes(G, 2)))
print(sorted(reachable_nodes(G, 5)))
print(len(G), len(reachable_nodes(G, 3)))

blocks.title: is_connected
blocks.prompt: Write is_connected(G): pick any starting node, find everything reachable from it, and compare with the size of the graph. reachable_nodes is defined.
blocks.tests:
assert is_connected(nx.complete_graph(5)) is True, "A complete graph is connected"
assert is_connected(nx.Graph([(0, 1), (2, 3)])) is False, "Two separate pairs are not connected"
G = nx.path_graph(6); G.add_node(99)
assert is_connected(G) is False, "One isolated node breaks connectivity"
assert is_connected(nx.path_graph(6)) is True, "A path is connected"
hints: next(iter(G)) gives you the first node of any graph.

blocks.title: A faster search
blocks.prompt: The book points out that reachable_nodes pushes a node onto the stack once for every edge that leads to it. Write reachable_nodes_precheck, which only pushes neighbours that aren't already seen, and returns the same set. It also returns how many pushes it made, so we can compare.
blocks.tests:
G = nx.complete_graph(20)
seen, pushes = reachable_nodes_precheck(G, 0)
assert seen == set(range(20)), "Should still find every node"
assert pushes <= 20, f"Each node should be pushed at most once; you made {pushes} pushes"
seen2, _ = reachable_nodes_precheck(nx.Graph([(0, 1), (1, 2), (5, 6)]), 0)
assert seen2 == {0, 1, 2}, f"Expected {{0, 1, 2}}, got {seen2}"
hints: Mark a node as seen the moment you push it, not when you pop it. Then the check if nb not in seen stops duplicates.
blocks.starter:
def reachable_nodes_precheck(G, start):
    seen = set()
    stack = [start]
    pushes = 1
    # your loop here
    return seen, pushes

blocks.html: In the ER model G(n, p), each possible pair of nodes gets an edge with probability p, independently. The book flips a biased coin for each pair.

blocks.title: flip, random_pairs, make_random_graph
blocks.prompt:
Write the three functions from the book:

  • flip(p) returns True with probability p (use np.random.random())
  • random_pairs(nodes, p) is a generator that yields each pair from all_pairs with probability p
  • make_random_graph(n, p) returns an ER graph with nodes 0 … n-1
blocks.tests:
np.random.seed(0)
assert abs(np.mean([flip(0.3) for _ in range(20000)]) - 0.3) < 0.02, "flip(0.3) should be True about 30% of the time"
assert make_random_graph(10, 1).number_of_edges() == 45, "With p=1 every pair is an edge"
assert make_random_graph(10, 0).number_of_edges() == 0, "With p=0 there are no edges"
assert make_random_graph(10, 0).number_of_nodes() == 10, "Nodes must exist even when there are no edges"
np.random.seed(1)
edges = np.mean([make_random_graph(30, 0.2).number_of_edges() for _ in range(40)])
assert abs(edges - 0.2 * 435) < 8, f"Expected about p * n(n-1)/2 = 87 edges on average, got {edges:.1f}"
hints: random_pairs looks exactly like all_pairs's caller: loop over all_pairs(nodes) and yield the edge only if flip(p).

blocks.q: In G(n, p) with n = 100 and p = 0.1, about how many edges do you expect?
blocks.why: There are 100·99/2 = 4950 possible pairs and each is an edge with probability 0.1, so you expect 495.

blocks.html: Erdős and Rényi found that connectivity doesn't rise smoothly with p. Below a critical value, ER graphs are almost never connected; just above it, they almost always are. For large n the critical value is about **p\* = ln(n) / n**.

blocks.title: Estimate the probability of being connected

blocks.html: Try n = 30 (and fewer iters if it feels slow). The jump gets sharper as n grows, and it moves to smaller p.

blocks.title: Rebuild prob_connected
blocks.prompt: From memory: write prob_connected(n, p, iters=100), the fraction of iters random graphs G(n, p) that are connected. make_random_graph and is_connected exist.
blocks.tests:
np.random.seed(2)
assert prob_connected(10, 1.0, 20) == 1.0, "With p=1 every graph is complete, so always connected"
assert prob_connected(10, 0.0, 20) == 0.0, "With p=0 no graph (of more than one node) is connected"
mid = prob_connected(20, np.log(20) / 20, 200)
assert 0.1 < mid < 0.7, f"At p* the probability should be somewhere in the middle, got {mid}"
hints: Build a list of True/False results, one per random graph, then use np.mean to turn it into a fraction.

blocks.q: Explain how reachable_nodes works, and why it can't loop forever even though the graph has cycles.
blocks.a:
• It keeps a stack of nodes still to process and a set of nodes already processed.
  • Each round it pops a node; if it's new it marks it seen and pushes all its neighbours.
  • Cycles lead back to nodes already in seen, which are popped and skipped, so each node is processed at most once and the loop ends when the stack is empty.
  • The graph is connected exactly when the set it returns contains every node.

blocks.q: What happens to the probability that G(n, p) is connected as p increases, and what's special about ln(n)/n?
blocks.a:
• It stays near 0 for small p, then jumps to near 1 over a narrow range of p: a phase transition.
  • The jump is centred near p\* = ln(n)/n, and it gets sharper as n grows.
  • Intuition: at p\*, the expected number of isolated nodes drops below about one; isolated nodes are the last thing stopping the graph from being connected.
